cur:monumental-san-vincenzo-crucifixion.summary: Christ, haloed, hangs on the cross with arms outstretched, wearing a loincloth, flanked by the Virgin at the left and Saint John at the right; at the foot of the cross kneels the small figure of Abbot Epiphanius with the square halo of the living, and below runs the inscription naming him. The painting is the devotional focus of a small vaulted crypt decorated under the abbot who ruled the monastery in 824–842.
facts: The crypt of Epiphanius belongs to the church of San Lorenzo in Insula at the great Benedictine abbey of San Vincenzo al Volturno, excavated in the 1980s by the San Vincenzo Project.
The abbey was richly favoured by Charlemagne, who granted it fiscal and jurisdictional privileges.

wga:zearly/1/2mural/4callist/callist6.summary: Painted in a roundel in an underground burial chamber, a young, beardless shepherd in a short tunic carries a lamb across his shoulders and a pail in his hand, while a bird and a sheep stand at his feet. Before Christians depicted Christ's face as a portrait, they most often pictured him this way: as the Good Shepherd who seeks the lost and lays down his life for his flock. Simple and tender, the image offered comfort to the faithful who buried their dead in the catacombs in an age of intermittent persecution.
facts: The Good Shepherd is the most common symbolic image of Christ in early Christian art in the Roman catacombs, and also appears on sarcophagi and in small statues.
The figure adapts a familiar Greco-Roman type, the kriophoros or 'ram-bearer', giving an established pagan motif a new Christian meaning.

The catacomb is named after Callixtus, who as a deacon is believed to have created it under Pope Zephyrinus (199–217) before becoming pope himself; it holds the 'Crypt of the Popes', where several third-century bishops of Rome were buried.
Here the shepherd also carries a pail, usually identified as a milk pail, which scholars have read as an allusion to the Eucharist or to spiritual nourishment.
wga:zearly/1/2mural/4callist/callist6.notes: WGA gives no chamber; the specific location within the catacomb (possibly the Crypts of Lucina area) was not confirmed.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/4nuovo/5t.summary: At the left, a bearded, haloed Christ in a dark purple mantle stands quietly, held by an elder from the crowd behind him. Facing him, Pilate sits on a cushioned judgement seat among his attendants, stretching out his hands over a basin held by a servant. The calm stillness of Christ beside the governor's gesture of self-exculpation gives the scene its quiet drama; it belongs to the Passion cycle along the upper wall of Theodoric's palace church.
facts: Only Matthew's Gospel records Pilate washing his hands before the crowd (Matthew 27:24).
In the Passion scenes of Sant'Apollinare Nuovo Christ is shown bearded, unlike the youthful beardless Christ of the miracle scenes on the opposite wall.
The mosaics were altered in the mid-19th century by the restorer Felice Kibel.
wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/4nuovo/5t.notes: WGA image is a cropped detail of the panel. Date refined from '6th century' to the Theodorician phase (before 526).

Q680128.summary: Christ's head, eyes closed and serene, is nearly swallowed by a crowd of grotesque, leering faces that fill the panel edge to edge. The contrast between his quiet acceptance and the surrounding cruelty makes the painting an intense meditation on innocence amid human malice. At lower left Saint Veronica, her eyes also closed, holds the veil bearing the imprint of his face.
facts: In 2015 the Bosch Research and Conservation Project attributed the panel to a follower rather than to Bosch himself; the Ghent museum still catalogues it under Bosch's name while noting that the attribution is disputed.
The two thieves appear at the right: the penitent thief, pale and harangued by a monk, at upper right, and the unrepentant one snarling at lower right.
Christ's head lies exactly where the two diagonals of the composition cross: the beam of the cross, and the line joining Veronica's veil to the penitent thief.

Q20809879.summary: A young man with long dark hair and a short beard turns his head gently, his eyes lowered in thought; there is no halo, only warm light falling on a humble, searching face. This small panel belongs to a group of studies of Christ that Rembrandt and his studio painted around 1648–56, apparently from a living model. Breaking with centuries of idealized types, these heads present a deeply human, inward Jesus.
facts: Rembrandt lived on the edge of Amsterdam's Jewish quarter, and it has often been suggested that the studies were painted from a young Jewish man of his neighborhood — a striking choice for depicting Jesus.
The inventory of Rembrandt's possessions in 1656 lists a 'head of Christ, done from life' (een Christus troni nae 't leven).
The heads are closely related to the Christ in Rembrandt's Supper at Emmaus of 1648 in the Louvre, and the Philadelphia face also recalls Christ in two of Rembrandt's prints of Christ preaching.

The group was reunited in the 2011 exhibition 'Rembrandt and the Face of Jesus' at the Louvre, Philadelphia Museum of Art and Detroit Institute of Arts; scholars continue to debate which heads are by Rembrandt's own hand.
